prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings placed B002 first, and I do not treat that as evidence of merit in itself. The merit is that the discovery is clear and the field visibly changed. Holst's work on GLP-1 secretion and action, Drucker's work on receptor biology and the intestinal and metabolic actions of proglucagon-derived peptides, and the identification of the active peptide form together established a mechanism that was then confirmed in large independent outcome trials. Impact has had time to become plain: type 2 diabetes and obesity are now treated through this pathway, with cardiovascular and renal benefit signals. A prize recognizes a specific discovery that changed a field, and this is one of the cleanest examples on the shortlist. A single-achievement prize for the physiology core, with three names, keeps the citation tied to discovery rather than product development.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Credit for identifying the active GLP-1 form is disputed, and I cannot resolve priority between Mojsov and other groups from the evidence supplied. The credited list also leaves out figures I would want to examine (for example Habener), so any trio is imperfect. Leaving out Knudsen means the prize would not recognize the long-acting analogue chemistry that made the drugs practical, and a critic could say the prize honors the physiology while skipping the step that delivered the benefit. Part of the impact is industrial, which fits a discovery prize awkwardly.

responses.point: Sandberg proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for B002, treating the arc from basic peptide biology to long-acting analogues as one complete story, and leaves out Mojsov because of the three-person limit and the disputed peptide-identification credit.
responses.response: I take the point that the complete arc is the attraction of this candidate, but I disagree with the choice. Dropping Mojsov removes one of the identification contributions that the physiology depends on, and the dispute over her credit is a reason to examine it carefully, not to omit her by default. Knudsen's contribution is real, but it is drug design resting on the discoveries, and the citation would then name a product-development step beside two discoverers. I would keep the three-person slot for the discovery side. If the committee decides that the analogue chemistry has to be recognized, then Knudsen displacing Mojsov is the least bad trade, and I agree with Sandberg that this is the actual decision on B002.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks B001 second and proposes Boyden, Nagel and Deisseroth, combining discovery of the channel with its demonstration in neurons, while noting that no clean three-person split exists.
responses.response: I agree that B001 is a strong candidate and that the discovery and neuronal-use steps both have to be represented. I qualify the trio. Leaving out Hegemann, whose channelrhodopsin characterization was decisive and who is credited alongside Nagel, and Bamberg, who shared the early biophysical work, is hard to defend on the supplied credit, and my own trio (Deisseroth, Hegemann, Nagel) also excludes Boyden. Each of these trios omits someone with a credible claim, so I regard B001 as more exposed to attribution objections than B002, even though the science is excellent. That is why I rank it as an alternative and not as the preferred choice.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks B002 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and says the main question is whether Knudsen's translational chemistry should displace a basic-physiology laureate.
responses.response: I agree with his three names and with his framing of the Knudsen question. Where I would add a qualification is that the unverified priority issue is not only about Knudsen. The identification of the active peptide is also unsettled, and he says he has not verified it. I would want the attribution review to settle that issue before we treat the trio as fixed, since a wrong choice here would be a visible error rather than a matter of taste.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks B002 first and B001 second, and places B017 (anti-TNF therapy, Feldmann and Maini) fourth, applying the same criteria to a candidate from her own clinical field.
responses.response: I did not include B017 among my top eight, so we differ. Anti-TNF therapy clearly defines cytokine-targeted treatment and the attribution is cleaner than for most candidates, which is a fair strength. My hesitation is the one she raises herself, discovery of a principle versus therapeutic development, and I rank it below the candidates where a basic discovery and its clinical consequence are both more clearly separated. I am open to hearing the case for it, but I would not move it into the preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Who should be credited for identifying the active GLP-1 form, and whether the evidence supports Mojsov's share.
Whether the omitted contributors, for example Habener, have claims strong enough to displace a name on the supplied list.
Whether a prize for B002 should include Knudsen in place of Mojsov, or neither of them.
Whether a two-part prize pairing B002 with B001 would be better than a single part, given the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted candidates from my profile. I worked with Ronald Evans on nuclear receptors, but he is not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I have co-authored with Per Svenningsson and once with Abdel El Manira, and these are general collaborations unrelated to the candidates discussed.
